abstract: Significance This study fundamentally advances our understanding of male reproductive biology by elucidating the essential roles of the telomeric whey acidic protein four-disulfide core (WFDC) gene cluster in spermatogenesis and sperm function. Using a comprehensive CRISPR/Cas9-based multigene knockout approach, we demonstrated that specific groups of WFDC genes are crucial for various periods of sperm development. Notably, our findings reveal that epididymal peptidase inhibitor (EPPIN) and its closest paralogs are indispensable for the progression from round spermatids to elongated spermatids, offering insights into the molecular mechanisms of sperm differentiation. These results not only reinforce EPPIN and its paralogs as viable nonhormonal male contraceptive targets, but also identify these genes as crucial candidates for enhanced genetic screening in the diagnosis of infertile men.
methods:
Materials and Methods
Ethics Statement.
Mice were maintained in accordance with NIH guidelines, and all animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Baylor College of Medicine (BCM).
Generation of WFDC KO Mice.
The 13 gene, 10 gene, 5 gene, 4 gene, and single
Wfdc3
KO mice were generated at BCM using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing. sgRNA target sequences were designed using the CRISPR direct suite and are listed in
SI Appendix
, Table S1
. Customized gRNAs were assembled into ribonucleoprotein complexes with Cas9 protein and electroporated into zygotes from superovulated B6D2F1 females. Embryos were cultured to the 2-cell stage and transferred into pseudopregnant CD1 females. Founder mutations were identified by PCR and Sanger sequencing, and mice were genotyped with PCR primers for WT and KO alleles as shown in
SI Appendix
, Table S1
. To expand each mutant line, B6D2 mice from an in-house colony were mated with F0 founder mice. Sexually mature male mice were used for phenotypic analysis. All mice were housed under standard conditions.
Analysis of the AR In Vitro Using RBGS Mice.
WFDC KO mice were crossed with B6D2 Tg mice carrying CAG/Su9-DsRed2 and Acr3-EGFP (RBGS) (
55
). Cauda epididymal spermatozoa were incubated in Toyoda Yokoyama Hosi medium at 37 °C under 5% CO
2
for up to 24 h. DAPI was added, and an aliquot of the sperm suspension was placed on a glass slide. AR rates were determined by observing enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) signals with a BX-53 microscope. Spermatozoa with EGFP signals in the acrosome were counted as acrosome intact. Images were taken after 15 min, 1 h, 2 h, 4 h, and 24 h. Over 100 spermatozoa were counted per trial.
Proteome Profiling of Testes Tissue.
Proteome profiling was conducted on whole testes tissue from 28-d-old KO and littermate control males (n = 5). Left and right sections of the reproductive tract were used as replicates, and 10 samples were submitted to the Mass Spectrometry Proteomics Core at BCM. Testes were dissected, weighed, frozen, and stored at −80 °C until submission. Protein lysis, digestion, tandem mass tag (TMT) labeling, and offline fractionation were performed as previously described (
56
), using LysC and Trypsin proteases. Peptides were desalted, labeled with TMT10 plex, and fractionated into 24 pooled fractions. Peptide fractions were analyzed using the Vanquish Neo ultra high performance liquid chromatography system coupled to an Orbitrap Eclipse mass spectrometer, with data acquired using the TMT MS2 method. Data processing followed previous protocols (
56
). The mouse protein database was downloaded from GENCODE (M32 release). MSFragger, MASIC, percolator, and iBAQ quantification parameters were as previously described (
56
). Median normalized and log10 transformed iBAQ values were used for analysis. Missing values were imputed, and differential analysis was performed using the moderated
t
test and log2 fold changes in the R package limma, with multiple-hypothesis testing corrected by the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure.
Statistical Analysis.
Statistical significance was evaluated using the two-tailed unpaired Student
t
test assuming unequal variances. For analyses involving 2 or more groups, One-Way ANOVA was used. Proteomics data were assessed using the moderated
t
test in the R package limma, with false discovery rate controlled by the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Data are represented as means ± SEM. Significance levels: *
P
< 0.05; **
P
< 0.01; ***
P
< 0.005; ****
P
< 0.0005; ns, not significant.
Additional materials and methods not listed here are provided in
SI Appendix
.

body:
As of today, global human population dynamics present a paradoxical challenge: while some countries experience rapid population growth, others, such as Japan, Germany, and Italy, face significant declines in birth rates. These demographic shifts underscore the diverse challenges and opportunities faced by different regions in managing population dynamics. This contrast highlights the need for the development of novel male contraceptives, diagnostic tools, and therapies for male infertility, which can address these varied demographic trends and enhance reproductive autonomy for men. In regions with rapid population growth, effective male contraceptives could alleviate pressures on resources and infrastructure, promoting sustainable development. Conversely, in countries grappling with declining birth rates, these innovations would provide women with additional choices and empower men to take a more active role in family planning, potentially leading to more balanced demographic trends. Expanding contraceptive options and improving infertility treatments for men by investigating genes required for male fertility is, therefore, crucial for achieving global reproductive health goals and fostering a more equitable distribution of reproductive responsibility. The current Food and Drug Administration-approved contraceptive options for men lag behind that of women, increasing the global interest in novel strategies of fertility management for men. Research confirms that the introduction of innovative, safe, and effective male contraceptives into the family planning market is widely accepted and represents progress toward reproductive justice, granting men additional choices to manage their fertility and share family planning responsibilities with their partners (
1
–
3
). Identifying genes required for male fertility is essential for progressing research on the development of the male contraceptive pill. In recent years, genetic studies using animal models have shown remarkable advancements identifying genes crucial for male fertility. However, further studies expanding our understanding of the intricate molecular mechanisms governing male fertility are fundamental for the development of novel safe and effective contraceptive solutions.
In recent years, extensive research on reproductive proteins has identified several promising candidate genes critical for the male reproductive system. Particularly noteworthy is epididymal protease inhibitor (EPPIN), which plays a vital role in sperm maturation and capacitation and has gained significant interest as a potential target for male contraception, with a single product identified, EP055 (
4
). The
EPPIN
gene is located on human chromosome 20, alongside a group of genes that express known protease inhibitor (PI) domains with homology to whey acidic protein (WAP) (
5
) (
Fig. 1
A
). This gene cluster codes for secreted proteins containing either one or more Kunitz domains and WAP domain typically in a configuration of 40 to 50 amino acids with eight conserved cysteine residues forming four disulfide bonds. This specific configuration is known as the WAP Four-Disulfide Core (WFDC) (
6
). In the human genome, a total of 18 WFDC genes have been discovered, of which, 16 WFDC genes are situated on two distinct loci on human chromosome 20 (
Fig. 1
B
). The centromeric locus contains four genes (
WFDC5
,
WFDC12
,
PI3,
and
SLPI
) while the telomeric locus contains 12 genes (
WFDC2
,
SPINT3
,
WFDC6
,
EPPIN
,
WFDC8
,
WFDC9
,
WFDC10A
,
WFDC11
,
WFDC10B
,
WFDC13
,
SPINT4
, and
WFDC3
) (
7
,
8
) (
Fig. 1
B
).
Fig. 1.
Evolutionary conservation of the WFDC locus. (
A
) Telomeric WFDC gene family phylogeny in humans and mice. The phylogenetic tree illustrates the structural domains of WFDC proteins, including WAP (green), Kunitz (blue), and SP (signal peptide; red) domains. The domain architecture, with associated amino acid counts, is shown for each gene family member. WFDC proteins exhibit a range of domain compositions, reflecting the functional diversity within the family. The left tree shows the phylogeny for human WFDC proteins, and the right tree shows the corresponding phylogeny for mouse WFDC proteins, highlighting the evolutionary relationships and domain configurations across species. This diagram was generated using the Clustal Omega Multiple Sequence Alignment program (
9
). Each branch represents paralogous proteins within the human and mouse clusters, with dendrogram distances reflecting their degree of dissimilarity. (
B
) Graphical representation of the WFDC gene loci on human chromosome 20 and mouse chromosome 2. The diagram illustrates evolutionary conservation in both centromeric and telomeric regions across species. The WFDC genes show syntenic relationships between humans and mice. Notable differences in gene spacing and subtle rearrangements in the gene order highlight species-specific adaptations while preserving overall genomic structure.
Despite 96 million years of evolution separating mice and humans (
10
), a remarkably conserved arrangement of orthologous genes is found on mouse Chromosome 2, with a similarly arranged centromeric cluster with five genes (
Wfdc5
,
Wfdc12
,
Wfdc15a
,
Wfdc15b
, and
Slpi
) and telomeric cluster with 14 genes (
Wfdc2
,
Spint3
,
Wfdc6a
,
Eppin
,
Wfdc8
,
Wfdc6b
,
Wfdc16
,
Wfdc9
,
Wfdc10
,
Wfdc11
,
Wfdc13
,
Spint4
,
Spint5
, and
Wfdc3
) (
11
) (
Fig. 1
B
). This high multigene locus conservation suggests a strong functional requirement and evolutionary pressure to maintain these genes as a set for male reproduction in primates and mammals. However, the specific involvement of the WFDC proteins in the male reproductive system has been highly speculative and based largely on their expression profiles. Research indicates that outside of the reproductive system, both the Kunitz and WAP domains are involved in protease inhibition, regulating various physiological processes (
12
,
13
). The Kunitz domain selectively inhibits several serine proteases, regulating proteolytic enzymes and preventing premature activation by binding their active sites (
14
,
15
). Similarly, WAP domain-containing proteins exhibit specificity toward certain serine proteases (
16
) and are abundant in mammalian reproductive tissues (
17
).
In our previous transcriptomics studies, we found that all genes belonging to the telomeric cluster, with exception of
WFDC2
, are reproductive tract specific or enriched in both mice and humans (
17
). In addition, previous studies demonstrated a differential region-specific expression of the centromeric and telomeric
Wfdc
genes during an innate inflammatory response induced by bacterial toxins in mouse epididymis (
18
). It has been postulated that evolutionary pressures stemming from reproductive challenges and exposure to microbial pathogens have likely driven the diversification of the
Wfdc
locus through duplication events, enabling the locus to assume a range of protective roles specific to different regions in the epididymis that safeguard both sperm and their functionality (
18
). While the exact functions of the WFDC proteins in sperm physiology have not been fully elucidated, their expression pattern and associations with fertility imply roles in sperm maturation, sperm–egg interactions, and other aspects of sperm function. In our previous studies, we ablated
Spint3
,
Spint4
, and
Spint5
in mice, revealing a functional requirement for
Spint4/5
, but not
Spint3
, in male mouse fertility, yielding valuable insight into the role of these genes (
17
). Further, despite the identification of EPPIN mutations linked to human male infertility, a mouse model to determine the physiological relevance of EPPIN alone has not yet been documented. Mouse
Eppin
, along with its closest paralogs,
Wfdc6a
and
Wfdc6b
, are recognized as orthologs to human EPPIN. Since multiple genes whose functions and expression are overlapping may compensate for the loss of any one gene, we hypothesize that the many WFDC genes in this gene cluster may partially or completely compensate for one another and that examination of multigene knockouts (KOs) could be vastly more informative in elucidating the physiological relevance of this gene cluster.
Our study aimed to define the functions of the 13 reproductive tract–specific or enriched WFDC genes located on mouse chromosome 2. We generated a 13 gene KO mouse model by deleting the genes from
Spint3
to
Wfdc3
(
Spint3, Wfdc6a, Eppin, Wfdc8, Wfdc6b, Wfdc16, Wfdc9, Wfdc10, Wfdc11, Wfdc13, Spint4, Spint5,
and
Wfdc3
), covering approximately 170 kb. Additionally, we generated a 10 gene KO model, spanning genes from
Spint3
to
Wfdc13
, and a 5 gene KO model spanning the coding region from
Wfdc16
to
Wfdc13
. These models allowed us to investigate the collective and differential impacts of these gene deletions. Further, we generated a 4 gene KO model, ablating
Eppin
and its closest paralogs (
Wfdc6a
,
Wfdc8
, and
Wfdc6b
) to investigate the functional requirement of
Eppin
in the absence of potential compensatory effects. Last, similar to our previously reported single KO of
Spint3
, we generated a single gene KO of
Wfdc3
to assess its specific role in male fertility. Our comprehensive approach successfully demonstrated the combined functional requirements of the telomeric WFDC genes, shedding significant light on their potential diverse yet pivotal roles in male reproductive health, their utility as diagnostic tools in the evaluation of infertile males, and their potential as contraceptive targets.
Results
Expression Profiles of Telomeric WFDC Locus Genes in Testes and Epididymides.
Through examination of our previous high-throughput transcriptomics datasets (
17
), we identified the entire telomeric WFDC locus in mice and humans as congruent in expression with nearly all genes restricted in expression to either the epididymis, testis, or both, except
WFDC2
/
Wfdc2
which displayed ubiquitous expression (
Fig. 2
A
and
SI Appendix
, Fig. S1
). To validate our transcriptomic findings and to explore the developmental gene expression profiles of
Eppin,
closely related
Wfdc6a
, and
Wfdc6b
, and closely localized
Wfdc8
gene, we conducted an expression analysis of each of these genes in testes and epididymides tissues of mice between the postnatal day (PND) 3 and 60 (
Fig. 2
B
). Our results revealed that
Eppin
exhibited a gradual increase in expression from PND 10 to 21 in the testes, with a slight decrease at PND 28 and 35, followed by a significant increase at PND 60 (
Fig. 2
B
). This suggests a potential requirement for
Eppin
in postmeiotic spermatid formation and differentiation in the testes. Notably, the expression of
Eppin
varied among distinct segments of the epididymis, showing significantly increased expression in the corpus epididymis at PND 21 and the highest expression in caput and corpus epididymis at PND 60, indicating its additional involvement in sperm maturation in the epididymis (
Fig. 2
B
). Surprisingly, the
Eppin
paralogs
Wfdc6a
and
Wfdc6b
demonstrated different expression profiles in both the testes and epididymides. Compared to
Eppin
and
Wfdc6b
,
Wfdc6a
consistently exhibited higher expression levels in the testes, gradually increasing from PND 3 to PND 21, with a slight decrease at PND 28 and 35, followed by a significant increase at PND 60 (
Fig. 2
B
). Interestingly, of the three paralogs
Wfdc6b
demonstrated the lowest expression levels in the testes between PND 3 and PND 60, and all the epididymal segments at PND 35 (
Fig. 2
B
). This differential expression pattern of
Eppin
and its paralogs likely indicates individual involvement of these genes at different stages of sperm development and maturation. Last, we found that
Wfdc8
demonstrated the lowest levels of expression in both testes and epididymides compared to
Eppin, Wfdc6a,
and
Wfdc6b
, with its expression highest in cauda epididymides at PND 21 (
Fig. 2
B
), possibly suggesting a different role in sperm maintenance or development. Taken together, these expression patterns suggest that the WFDC proteins function at various stages in sperm development and maturation in the testes and epididymides, respectively, likely by regulating proteolytic activity of key reproductive proteases.
Fig. 2.
Expression profile of the telomeric WFDC genes. (
A
) Comparative graphical visualization of WFDC gene expression levels from a reanalysis of hundreds of previously published mouse RNA-seq datasets, focusing on mouse reproductive tissues: testes, caput (cap), corpus (cor), and cauda (cau) epididymis, and combined nonreproductive (non-repro) tissues. Varying shades from white to red indicate a gradient of gene expression levels, from white, corresponding to minimal or no expression, to red, corresponding to a high level of expression. (
B
) Agarose gel electrophoresis (2% agarose) of PCR amplified products using mouse-specific PCR primer sets and cDNA extracted from testes and segments of epididymis showing gene expression profiles of
Eppin
and its orthologous
Wfdc6a
, and
Wfdc6b
, and closely localized
Wfdc8
in mice of PND 3 through 60.
Gapdh
was used as a housekeeping gene.
Generation of Multigene Wfdc KO Mice.
We have previously identified the functional requirement of
Spint4
and
Spint5
in male fertility in mice (
17
). Human studies and translational studies with mice recognized EPPIN as a key protein regulating sperm motility after ejaculation (
19
,
20
). As illustrated in
Fig. 3
, to systematically investigate the male reproductive requirement and potential functional role of the remainder of the genes within the
Wfdc
locus, we utilized our previously described CRISPR/Cas9 Electroporation of Zygotes gene editing technology to generate several KO mouse lines deleting 13, 10, 5, 4, and 1 gene(s) within the telomeric region of interest on mouse chromosome 2. Guided by custom designed singleguide RNA (sgRNA) molecules, each of the KO lines resulted in deletions of differing sizes and genomic targets. Genotyping and Sanger sequencing results confirmed that the 13 gene KO founders harbored a 173.2 kb pair deletion corresponding to the genes
Spint3
,
Wfdc6a
,
Eppin
,
Wfdc8
,
Wfdc6b
,
Wfdc16
,
Wfdc9
,
Wfdc10
,
Wfdc11
,
Wfdc13
,
Spint4
,
Spint5
,
Wfdc3
(
Fig. 3
and
SI Appendix
, Fig. S2
). The 10 gene KO resulted in a 115.4 kb deletion corresponding to the genes from
Spint3
to
Wfdc13
(
Fig. 3
and
SI Appendix
, Fig. S3
), the 5 gene KO founders contained a 46.7 kb deletion from
Wfdc16
to
Wfdc13
(
Fig. 3
and
SI Appendix
, Fig. S4
), and the 4 gene KO contained a 28.8 kb deletion from
Wfdc6a
to
Wfdc6b
(
Fig. 3
and
SI Appendix
, Fig. S5
). In addition to the multigene KO, we generated and expanded a single KO of
Wfdc3
containing a −48/+2 bp indel from within exon 1 to intron 1 resulting in a premature stop codon truncating the WFDC3 protein to its first 13 amino acids followed by a single degenerate histidine amino acid (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S8
A
). The sgRNA target sequences for each of the mutant lines are provided in
SI Appendix
, Table S1
. Specific primers for wild-type (WT) and KO alleles were designed as listed in
SI Appendix
, Table S1
and used for subsequent genotyping. After expanding each of the multigene deletion lines to obtain homozygous mice, we confirmed the respective large deletions through long-read whole genome sequencing using Oxford Nanopore Technologies’ PromethION platform (
SI Appendix
, Figs. S2
B
–S5
B
).
Fig. 3.
CRISPR/Cas9 strategy for generating multigene WFDC KO mice. Schematic representation of the telomeric WFDC locus on mouse chromosome 2, with arrows indicating the 5′-3′ orientation of each gene. Deleted genes in each KO line are marked in red, showing a 13 gene deletion between
Spint3
and
Wfdc3
, a 10 gene deletion between
Spint3
and
Wfdc13
, a five gene deletion between
Wfdc16
and
Wfdc13
, and a four gene deletion between
Wfdc6a
and
Wfdc6b
. Exons involved in each deletion are depicted, along with the locations of each gRNA and Cas9 cleavage sites, indicated by black lightning bolts. Genotyping primers (forward [Fw] and reverse [Rv]) and their orientations are marked with red arrows. The size of each multigene deletion is shown in red text. A 1-kb scale is provided for reference.
Lack of Multiple Genes within the Telomeric Wfdc Gene Cluster Results in Pleiotropic Effects on Sperm Development.
To investigate the functional consequences of ablating the WFDC PIs in the male reproductive system, we conducted a parallel analysis of the reproductive tract phenotype of the multiple and single gene KO mice. This investigation encompassed the assessment of the development of the reproductive organs and progression of spermatogenesis. Our results revealed that none of the KO strains generated in this study displayed any overtly abnormal appearance, differences in body weight (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S6
A
), body composition, or difference in behavior when compared to their littermate controls. To determine whether the mutant mice experienced defects in the development of the reproductive organs, we performed a gross analysis of whole testes and epididymides and found no significant difference in epididymis weights in any of the KO lines (
SI Appendix
, Figs. S6
A
and S8
B
). While the 5 gene KO, and single
Wfdc3
KO males exhibited comparably normal gross testis morphology, we noted significant decreases in testis sizes and weights in the 13 gene, 10 gene, and 4 gene KO mice compared to their littermate controls (
Fig. 4
A
and
SI Appendix
, Fig. S8
B
).
Fig. 4.
Deletion of multiple WFDC genes results in spermatogenic defects in mice. (
A
) Gross morphology of reproductive organs from 16-wk-old homozygous WFDC KO males and WT littermates. A significant decrease in testis size and weight is observed in the 13 gene, 10 gene, and 4 gene KO males compared to WT. Asterisks denote levels of statistical significance: *
P
< 0.05; **
P
< 0.01; ***
P
< 0.005; ****
P
< 0.0005. (
B
) Histological analysis of the testes and epididymal segments (caput, corpus, cauda) from homozygous WFDC KO and WT littermates. Bouin’s fixed, 4-μm longitudinal sections of the epididymis and transverse sections of the testes were stained with PAS-hematoxylin.
Insets
(
Right
) highlight magnified regions from each tissue section (
Left
). KO mice with 13, 10, and 4 gene deletions exhibit significantly reduced epithelial thickness, diffuse multinucleated giant cells (blue arrows), and undifferentiated round spermatids (blue arrowheads) in the testicular and epididymal lumens. Compared to WT and 5 gene KO mice, no elongated spermatids or mature spermatozoa were detected in the 13, 10, or 4 gene KO mice. Scale bars (black) represent 60 μm.
Following these findings, to investigate any structural defects in tissue morphology and composition, we performed a thorough histomorphometric analysis of the longitudinal sections of all segments of the epididymis and transverse sections of the testis (
Fig. 4
B
and
SI Appendix
, Fig. S8
C
). Our analysis did not reveal any obvious defects in tissue morphology or composition of the testes or epididymides in the 5 gene KO (
Fig. 4
B
) and
Wfdc3
KO (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S8
C
). The increase in testis weight observed in the 5 gene KO is not statistically significant (
Fig. 4
A
). Therefore, the slight increase in testis weight does not appear to indicate a significant role in apoptosis or other pathological processes. In contrast, the 13 gene, 10 gene, and 4 gene KOs were azoospermic, displaying the presence of round, but not elongated spermatids, and significantly reduced epithelial thickness of the seminiferous tubule (
Fig. 4
B
). An abundance of immature germ cells including round spermatids was also consistently found in the lumen of caput, corpus, and cauda epididymides of 13 gene, 10 gene, and 4 gene KOs (
Fig. 4
B
). Moreover, we observed changes in the diameter of the epididymal lumen, and changes in epididymis tubule epithelium height. We observed numerous intraepithelial clear vacuoles and hyperplastic alterations in the epithelium, typical of epididymal cribriform hyperplasia (blue arrows in
Fig. 4
B
). Further, the 13 gene, 10 gene, and 4 gene KO mice exhibited the presence of diffuse multinucleated giant cells in both the seminiferous epithelium and the epididymal lumen, indicative of increased germ cell degradation, consistent with the darker Periodic Acid-Shiff (PAS) staining across the KO tissue sections (
Fig. 4
B
). These histological changes strongly suggest disruptions in sperm differentiation and increased apoptosis. To determine whether the observed tissue degradation was a result of increased inflammation, we conducted immunohistochemistry studies using the panhematopoietic cell marker CD45. In both WT and KO mice with multiple WFDC gene deletions, CD45+ immune cells were primarily scattered throughout the interstitium of the caput and cauda epididymis. However, no significant difference in the immune cell abundance was observed between WT and KO mice (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S6
B
).
To investigate the effect of multigene ablation of WFDC family members on sperm maturation and function we conducted computer-assisted sperm analysis (CASA) of sperm isolated from cauda epididymides of 16-wk-old KO and WT males. We assessed the key sperm parameters of sperm count, motility, hyperactivation, and progressive motility (
Fig. 5
A
) across the experimental and control groups. As expected, the single
Wfdc3
KO sperm exhibited characteristics comparable to those of WT sperm with normal sperm count and motility (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S8
D
). To the contrary, the 4 gene KO mice presented with complete azoospermia phenocopying the larger 13 gene and 10 gene deletant mice (
Fig. 5
A
), thus narrowing down the key genes driving the spermiogenesis defect. Despite normal testes and epididymides morphology as shown in
Fig. 4
, and no significant decrease in sperm cell count, the 5 gene KO males displayed a significant reduction in sperm motility and progressive motility compared to their WT littermates (
Fig. 5
A
). To investigate whether the decreased sperm motility parameters stemmed from an increased cell death or a structural defect in the 5 gene KO mice, we conducted a live/dead cell assay followed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis of 16-wk-old KO and WT littermates (
Fig. 5
B
and
C
). Our findings revealed that the percentage of live sperm from 5 gene KO mice was significantly lower (
P
value < 0.001) than that of their WT counterparts (
Fig. 5
B
), which is congruent with the observed decrease in sperm motility and progressive motility. Further, our SEM analysis of sperm morphology showed an increased incidence of irregularities in the helical structure of sperm mitochondria as shown in the midpiece of 5 gene KO sperm (
Fig. 5
C
), which is likely a consequence of defects in later stages of sperm development and maturation. To further investigate structural defects and their impact on sperm–oocyte interaction, we analyzed the acrosome reaction (AR) of sperm in vitro. We crossed our 5 gene KO mouse model with RBGS (red body, green sperm) mice expressing fluorescent markers, as detailed in the
Materials and Methods
section, to visualize sperm acrosomes and mitochondria. Using fluorescence imaging, we assessed the AR capability of the sperm at various time points during a 15-min to 24-h incubation in capacitation media. Our analysis demonstrated a significant increase in acrosome-reacted sperm in the 5 gene KO mice after 15 min and 1 h of incubation (
Fig. 5
D
). These findings indicate that sperm from the 5 gene KO mice likely undergo premature AR likely due to a combination of structural defects and other multifactorial influences. Taken together, these findings suggest that the telomeric WFDC gene cluster on mouse chromosome 2 has pleiotropic effects on sperm development.

Multigene WFDC KO Male Mice Are Infertile due to Defects in Sperm Development and Maturation.
To investigate the functional consequence of the observed phenotype and reproductive requirement of the telomeric WFDC gene cluster in male fertility, the 13 gene KO, 10 gene KO, 5 gene KO, 4 gene KO, single
Wfdc3
KO, and WT littermate adult males (6 to 7 wk of age) were each housed continuously with two WT females for three months and the size and number of litters was recorded. The
Wfdc3
KO males sired a number and size of litters during the test mating period that was not significantly different from the control males (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S8
E
), while the 13 gene KO, 10 gene KO, and 4 gene KO males sired zero litters over the entire test mating period (
Fig. 6
A
). The 5 gene KO males exhibited a statistically significant 91% reduction in the number of pups sired per male per month, and a statistically significant 75% reduction in litter size over the initial 3-mo mating period (n = 3 controls, n = 7 KOs) (
Fig. 6
A
). Three of the seven 5 gene KO males were completely infertile throughout the assessment, while one male consistently sired one pup per litter and one litter per month for the entire 3-mo period. The remaining three KO males showed reduced fertility, producing smaller litters in the second month but no litters in the third month. In contrast, all control males continued to sire litters throughout the entire 3-mo period. To assess whether fertility further declines with age in the 5 gene KO males, we conducted an additional 3-mo fertility trial using 6-mo-old KO and control males at the start of mating. In this second trial, the 5 gene KO males showed an even more pronounced decline, with a statistically significant 99% reduction in the number of pups sired per male per month and a 94% reduction in litter size (n = 4 controls, n = 2 KOs) (
Fig. 6
A
). Across each of the multigene deletant lines, heterozygous male and female mice exhibited normal fertility with no obvious defects in development and health. This suggests that dosage effects are not significant and that heterozygous individuals have sufficient levels of the deleted WFDCs to maintain normal reproductive function. Across each of the multigene deletant lines, homozygous null females also demonstrated normal fertility. We confirmed this by routinely using heterozygous and homozygous null females interchangeably for colony maintenance and finding no difference in the average number of litters or pup per litter produced (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S7
C
).

Given the significant decreases in sperm motility, sperm viability, and fecundity seen in 5 gene KO males, we evaluated their fertilization potential through in vitro fertilization (IVF) assay. Sperm extracted from cauda epididymides were capacitated in human tubular fluid medium prior to insemination. Oocytes from superovulated females were harvested and coincubated with the capacitated sperm for 24 h to allow fertilization and development to the 2-cell stage. Our analysis showed that the 5 gene KO mice produced, on average, 55% fewer 2-cell stage embryos compared to their WT littermates (

To investigate whether the decreased fertilization potential in the 5 gene KO mice stemmed from defects in sperm–oocyte binding, we assessed the abundance and processing (activation) of a key sperm surface protein ADAM3, known to be crucial for sperm zona pellucida (ZP) binding. The immunoblot analysis on protein extracts from testes and epididymides tissue from the 5 gene KO mice revealed that unprocessed ADAM3 levels in the testes were similar between WT and KO mice, whereas the levels of activated ADAM3 in the epididymis were reduced in the KO mice (

SI Appendix

B
). These results indicate a potential deficiency in ADAM3 processing or increased ADAM3 degradation in the epididymis during sperm maturation in the absence of PIs encoded by the deleted WFDC genes. This deficiency, coupled with decreased sperm viability and structural irregularities in sperm mitochondrial structure, likely contributes to male infertility of the 5 gene KO males. This KO set, which has the same level of functional necessity as the 10 and 13 gene sets, helps narrow down the genes responsible for the severe azoospermia phenotype present in 10 and 13 gene Kos (

Testes Proteome Profiling of the Four Gene WFDC KO Mice.
Since the 4 gene KO mice lack the PIs encoded by the
Wfdc6a
,
Eppin
,
Wfdc8
, and
Wfdc6b
genes, we aimed to elucidate the specific molecular mechanisms responsible for the severe phenotype in adults characterized by impaired differentiation of round spermatids into elongated spermatids. Spermatogenesis in mice begins shortly after birth with prospermatogonia migrating to the basement membrane of the seminiferous tubules by PND 6, differentiating into primitive type A spermatogonia (
22
). By PND 8, type A and type B spermatogonia appear, initiating spermatogonial proliferation through mitotic divisions (
23
). Meiotic prophase begins by PND 10 with the emergence of preleptotene and leptotene spermatocytes, progressing through zygotene and pachytene stages by PND 14 (
23
). By PND 18, secondary spermatocytes and round spermatids are present, leading to spermiogenesis (
23
). Mature spermatozoa appear in the seminiferous tubules by PND 35, completing the first wave of spermatogenesis (
23
). To identify direct targets affected by the combined absence of the WFDC6A, EPPIN, WFDC8, and WFDC6B proteins, and to avoid confounding effects from the absence of elongated spermatids in adult mice with severely disrupted spermatogenesis, we conducted our proteome profiling at PND 28, when elongated spermatids are just beginning to develop in the testes. Our proteomics analysis unveiled changes in the levels of various proteins in the 4 gene KO testes in comparison to WT testes. The 50 most significantly up- and downregulated proteins are listed in
SI Appendix
, Fig. S9
A
, and the full list of proteins and peptide counts revealed through our analyses of the data are available in
Dataset S1
. The entire mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD053290. Among the most significantly increased proteins in the KO testes, we found proteins associated with protein degradation (TXNDC16, UGGT2, MSL2, and PSMG4), and apoptosis regulators [fas associated via death domain (FADD)] (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S9
). Upregulation of proteins involved in protein degradation is consistent with the severe phenotype observed in the 4 gene KO. Moreover, we noted a significant upregulation of transcription factors ZFY1, and ZFY2, associated with meiotic recombination checkpoint signaling and spermatid development, indicating a compensatory response to increased germ cell malfunction or loss (
SI Appendix
, Figs. S9 and S10
). Likewise, the increases in additional spermatogenesis associated proteins (FAM221B, STRA8, CCDC42, and SPATA25) in KO testes indicate a compensatory response to the failure to properly form spermatids (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S9
A
). Among the most significantly decreased proteins in the testes of the 4 gene KO mice we found several proteins involved in transcriptional and epigenetic regulation (MED7, EZH2), cell structure and cytoskeletal organization (KANK4, CML1), proteostasis and protein degradation (PDCL, GGCT), cell signaling and regulatory functions (SHOX2, TSPYL1), and other spermatogenesis and sperm function roles (SRM, SPATS1) (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S9
A
). Downregulation of epigenetic modulators (EZH2) and changes in transcription factor levels (MED7) could lead to inappropriate gene expression patterns during spermatid maturation. Changes in proteins involved in cell structure, proteostasis, signaling, and spermatogenesis functions suggest a broader disruption of cellular homeostasis and function in spermatids. While we found through additional RNA-seq studies that our previously published
Spint4/Spint5
double KO did not lead to changes in expression of any of the other WFDC genes, without further testing we cannot rule out the possibility that the decreased levels of WFDC10 in the 4 gene KO are a result of disruption of a
Wfdc10
cis-regulatory element.
Further, we performed immunoblot analyses of key proteins associated with sperm development and function and found significantly decreased signals specific to ADAM3 and TSSK3 in the testes of 4 gene KO mice (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S10
). Taken together, these findings indicate that the impaired differentiation of round spermatids into elongated spermatids in the 4 gene KO mice is associated with significant upregulation of proteins involved in protein degradation, cell cycle regulation, and compensatory responses to germ cell death, alongside downregulation of various structural, regulatory, and spermatogenesis-associated proteins. This comprehensive level of disruption, present at a timepoint (PND 28) when no significant histological changes are evident, underscores the critical roles of the deleted WFDC genes in maintaining cellular homeostasis and proper spermatid differentiation.
Discussion
In our study, we aimed to advance the field of male contraception and reproductive health by elucidating the functional roles of WFDC genes expressed in the male reproductive tract. To achieve this, we employed a multiple gene KO approach, deviating from the traditional single-gene KO methodology. This methodology was grounded in the recognition that the intricate network of processes underpinning male fertility often involves a cohort of partially redundant proteins working in tandem, a complexity that may be understated by single-gene studies. The WFDC gene family, known for their contributions to sperm maturation and protective immunity, exhibit high evolutionary conservation and homology among their members (
Fig. 1
), and demonstrate abundant expression in male reproductive tissues across different species (
Fig. 2
). Despite significant interest in EPPIN as a male contraceptive target and a study demonstrating that human mutations in
EPPIN
are associated with male infertility (
24
), a null mouse KO model of
Eppin
has not been described. However, the examination of a WFDC gene such as
Eppin,
in isolation, may inadequately represent the collective influence of its closest paralogs on sperm development and function. Understanding the consequences of knocking out multiple closely related genes provides a clearer picture of the functional role of a gene family when numerous factors including redundant pathways, compensatory mechanisms, and epigenetic modifications governs single gene impacts.
In our comprehensive study of multiple genes within the telomeric WFDC locus and their impact on male reproductive performance, we demonstrate the indispensable role of the WFDC genes in spermatogenesis and sperm function. As anticipated, our single gene KO of
Wfdc3
demonstrated no phenotypic consequences (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S8
), just as our previously reported single gene KO of
Spint3
demonstrated none (
17
). However, and significantly, our 5 gene KO exhibited severe oligoasthenoteratozoospermia and infertility, characterized by defects in acrosome reactivity and sperm viability. In contrast, our 4 gene KO, as well as the 10 gene and 13 gene KOs that included these four genes, demonstrated azoospermia and sterility due to a complete absence of elongated spermatids. This effect in the 4, 10, and 13 genes KOs was concomitant with significant degeneration of the seminiferous tubule epithelium, a prevalence of immature germ cells throughout the epididymal lumen, and significantly reduced testes sizes (
Fig. 4
). Given that our findings with the 4 gene, 10 gene, and 13 gene KOs demonstrated a consistent phenotype across all three lines, we conclude that the genes driving the severe phenotype resides within the 4 gene KO:
Wfdc6a
,
Eppin
,
Wfdc8
, and
Wfdc6b
. Since our prior research showed that the combination of
Spint4
and
Spint5
in mice is indispensable for sperm function, and our current research shows that the non-overlapping sets of genes within the 4 gene and 5 gene KO lines are essential for male fertility, albeit with varying points of impact, our studies collectively establish the critical role of WFDC proteins in sperm production, maturation, and function across the male reproductive tract.
Decades of research shows that from the initial formation of spermatozoa within the seminiferous tubule of the testis to the subsequent sperm maturation in the epididymis, the maintenance of normal sperm function involves a complex and coordinated mechanism involving various proteases and their corresponding inhibitors. Numerous serine proteases have been identified to play a pivotal role within the male reproductive tract (
25
–
30
). Additionally, endogenous inhibitors of these proteases synthesized within male reproductive tissues and fluids, regulate protease activity including production, degradation, and activation (
31
,
32
). In humans, serine protease inhibitory activity of EPPIN has been previously demonstrated to modulate the hydrolysis of a semenogelin protein 1 by KLK3/PSA (a serine protease), playing a pivotal role in sperm maturation and providing antimicrobial protection for spermatozoa in the ejaculate coagulum (
33
,
34
). Similarly, based on sequence homology, WFDC6 is predicted to inhibit serine-type endopeptidase activity in the male reproductive tract. Combined with histological analysis, our proteome profiling testis tissue from the 4 gene KO—lacking the activity of EPPIN, WFDC6A, WFDC6B, and WFDC8—highlights the consequence of disrupting the protease-to-PI balance during spermatogenesis. Here, we demonstrate that the absence of the WFDC PIs encoded within the four gene locus leads to a cascade of events likely resulting from unregulated protease activity. This phenomenon is evident through increased levels of proteins associated with protein degradation and quality control, such as TXNDC16, UGGT2, MSL2, and PSMG4 (
35
–
39
) (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S9
). Unwanted protein activity likely causes cellular damage and death, leading to altered epigenetic and transcriptional responses, further disrupting spermiogenesis and other processes, culminating in spermatogenic failure in the 4 gene, 10 gene, and 13 gene KOs. This is supported by the upregulation of FADD, an apoptosis regulator, initiating cellular degradation and an inflammatory response. This disruption is further indicated by the upregulation of tetraspanin 18 (TSPAN18) and the downregulation of epigenetic modulators CML1 (NAT8) and EZH2, as well as transcription factors like MED7 (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S9
and
Dataset S1
). Additionally, we observed decreased levels of proteins involved in mitochondrial function, protein synthesis, cellular structure, cell differentiation, and spermatogenesis, such as GGCT, SHOX2, PDCL, CML1, KANK4, SRM, SPATS1. As summarized in
Fig. 7
, this progressively degenerative cascade is likely a downstream effect of increased protease activity due to the absence of WFDC PIs during spermatogenesis.

Furthermore, our study reveals a notable reduction in the levels of testicular ADAM3 and TSSK3, essential proteins previously implicated in normal sperm development and function. While direct interaction between ADAM3, TSSK3, and WFDC proteins was not demonstrated, it is plausible that the absence of regulation by WFDC PIs leads to increased protease activity, resulting in premature or abnormal cleavage and degradation of pivotal proteins such as ADAM3 and TSSK3. Our observations in the 5 gene KO mice, which exhibit apparently normal sperm differentiation but a marked decrease in activated ADAM3 levels in the epididymis, further support this notion. The consequential reduction in sperm fertilization potential, shown in
SI Appendix
, Fig. S7
, underscores the significance of WFDC genes located between
Wfdc16
and
Wfdc13
in modulating later stages of sperm development and maturation. Specifically, these genes likely play a crucial role in processing key sperm surface proteins necessary for successful sperm–oocyte binding and fertilization.
Our study generated multiple WFDC KO mouse models by specifically targeting the highly conserved telomeric region of mouse chromosome 2 to investigate their pleiotropic effects on male fertility. These models displayed a spectrum of phenotypes, ranging from complete azoospermia to decreased sperm motility and viability, as well as mitochondrial structural irregularities, highlighting the pleiotropic nature of these genetic alterations.
In the 13, 10, and 4 gene deletion models, we observed a pronounced testicular phenotype characterized by an arrest in sperm differentiation. Due to the severity of this phenotype, it was difficult to specifically investigate the roles of these genes in the epididymis within these KO models. However, given the strong expression of WFDC proteins in both the testes and epididymis, it is likely that these proteins play crucial roles in regulating the local immune response and maintaining epithelial integrity in the epididymis. This is further supported by the structural changes observed in the epididymal epithelium of these KO mice, suggesting that WFDC proteins may mediate defense mechanisms or control the microenvironment required for proper sperm development.
In contrast, the 5 gene KO model exhibited normal sperm differentiation in the testes but demonstrated defects in sperm structure and function during the maturation process in the epididymis. This indicates that the genes within this region are critical for modulating the epididymal environment, particularly influencing sperm maturation and membrane remodeling. Supporting this, we observed a marked decrease in activated ADAM3 levels in the epididymis of the 5 gene KO mice, despite apparently normal testicular sperm differentiation. This reduction in ADAM3 levels is associated with decreased sperm fertilization potential (
SI Appendix
, Fig. S7
), underscoring the importance of WFDC genes between
Wfdc16
and
Wfdc13
in modulating later stages of sperm maturation.
Additionally, in the 13, 10, and 4 gene KO mice we observed a notable reduction in the levels of testicular ADAM3 and TSSK3, essential proteins for normal sperm development and function. Although a direct interaction between ADAM3, TSSK3, and WFDC proteins was not demonstrated, it is plausible that the absence of regulation by WFDC PIs leads to increased protease activity. This could result in premature or abnormal cleavage and degradation of pivotal proteins such as ADAM3 and TSSK3, mirroring how pathogens exploit proteases to facilitate infection.
Pathogens involved in reproductive tract infections, such as
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
,
Chlamydia trachomatis
, and
Trichomonas vaginalis
, produce or exploit proteases to degrade host tissues, evade immune responses, and promote invasion. Common proteases include metalloproteases, cysteine proteases, and serine proteases, which degrade extracellular matrix components and immune proteins (
40
–
44
). Additionally, specific proteases like IgA1 protease and mucin-degrading proteases help pathogens disrupt mucosal barriers and neutralize immunoglobulins (
45
–
49
). Some pathogens also hijack host proteases, such as plasmin, to enhance tissue destruction and facilitate their spread (
50
).
WFDC proteins, particularly members like secretory leukocyte PI (SLPI) and elafin, play a crucial role in inhibiting both host and pathogen-derived proteases, which pathogens may otherwise exploit for infection. For instance, SLPI and elafin are known to inhibit neutrophil elastase (a serine protease), which certain pathogens like
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
can exploit to degrade host tissues during infection. By inhibiting elastase, WFDC proteins limit the tissue damage that would facilitate pathogen invasion. Additionally, they modulate immune responses, reducing excessive inflammation that could aid pathogen dissemination (
51
–
54
). Moreover, WFDC proteins have been shown to possess antimicrobial properties and can directly influence host–pathogen interactions, adding another layer of defense during infections, particularly in epithelial tissues such as those in the reproductive tract (
7
,
34
).
Besides likely protecting the testis and epididymis epithelium and sperm from damages induced by aberrant immature germ cell and sperm protease activities, this positions WFDC proteins as critical mediators in maintaining the balance between immune protection and tissue integrity during infection or damage.
Overall, these findings highlight the complex and crucial role of WFDC genes in male fertility and immune defense, particularly in regulating protease activity, maintaining the epididymal microenvironment, and ensuring proper sperm maturation. The molecular mechanisms through which WFDC PIs exert their regulatory functions in the male reproductive tract and their individual involvement warrant further investigation. Understanding these mechanisms could provide valuable insights into therapeutic targets for male infertility and the prevention of sexually transmitted infections.
Conclusions
In summary, our studies elucidate the role of WFDC genes in male fertility and infertility, advancing our understanding of their implications for male contraceptive development initiatives. By employing a KO strategy targeting a closely related gene family, we provided definitive genetic evidence supporting longstanding hypotheses regarding the functions of WFDC locus genes, particularly in relation to EPPIN as a contraceptive target (
4
). Our findings underscore that alterations within the WFDC gene cluster can lead to similar or overlapping phenotypic outcomes due to their functional interconnectedness and shared regulatory mechanisms. Specifically, we demonstrated the essential roles of various WFDC genes at different stages of sperm development and male fertility.
Eppin
, alongside its orthologs
Wfdc6a
and
Wfdc6b
, and
Wfdc8
, were found to be indispensable for the progression from round spermatids to elongated spermatids. Meanwhile, the locus encompassing
Wfdc16
,
Wfdc9
,
Wfdc10
,
Wfdc11
, and
Wfdc13
is indispensable for sperm maturation and function. These findings highlight the intricate genetic interactions within gene clusters and illustrate how changes in one gene can affect multiple biological processes, resembling pleiotropy. Furthermore, our results suggest that various WFDC genes play critical roles in sperm development by modulating the activity of key serine proteases in the male reproductive tract. Beyond their contraceptive potential, these findings hold therapeutic promise for diagnosing and treating men with idiopathic male infertility linked to mutations within the evolutionarily conserved WFDC locus on human chromosome 20.
Materials and Methods
Ethics Statement.
Mice were maintained in accordance with NIH guidelines, and all animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Baylor College of Medicine (BCM).
Generation of WFDC KO Mice.
The 13 gene, 10 gene, 5 gene, 4 gene, and single
Wfdc3
KO mice were generated at BCM using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing. sgRNA target sequences were designed using the CRISPR direct suite and are listed in
SI Appendix
, Table S1
. Customized gRNAs were assembled into ribonucleoprotein complexes with Cas9 protein and electroporated into zygotes from superovulated B6D2F1 females. Embryos were cultured to the 2-cell stage and transferred into pseudopregnant CD1 females. Founder mutations were identified by PCR and Sanger sequencing, and mice were genotyped with PCR primers for WT and KO alleles as shown in
SI Appendix
, Table S1
. To expand each mutant line, B6D2 mice from an in-house colony were mated with F0 founder mice. Sexually mature male mice were used for phenotypic analysis. All mice were housed under standard conditions.
Analysis of the AR In Vitro Using RBGS Mice.
WFDC KO mice were crossed with B6D2 Tg mice carrying CAG/Su9-DsRed2 and Acr3-EGFP (RBGS) (
55
). Cauda epididymal spermatozoa were incubated in Toyoda Yokoyama Hosi medium at 37 °C under 5% CO
2
for up to 24 h. DAPI was added, and an aliquot of the sperm suspension was placed on a glass slide. AR rates were determined by observing enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) signals with a BX-53 microscope. Spermatozoa with EGFP signals in the acrosome were counted as acrosome intact. Images were taken after 15 min, 1 h, 2 h, 4 h, and 24 h. Over 100 spermatozoa were counted per trial.
Proteome Profiling of Testes Tissue.
Proteome profiling was conducted on whole testes tissue from 28-d-old KO and littermate control males (n = 5). Left and right sections of the reproductive tract were used as replicates, and 10 samples were submitted to the Mass Spectrometry Proteomics Core at BCM. Testes were dissected, weighed, frozen, and stored at −80 °C until submission. Protein lysis, digestion, tandem mass tag (TMT) labeling, and offline fractionation were performed as previously described (
56
), using LysC and Trypsin proteases. Peptides were desalted, labeled with TMT10 plex, and fractionated into 24 pooled fractions. Peptide fractions were analyzed using the Vanquish Neo ultra high performance liquid chromatography system coupled to an Orbitrap Eclipse mass spectrometer, with data acquired using the TMT MS2 method. Data processing followed previous protocols (
56
). The mouse protein database was downloaded from GENCODE (M32 release). MSFragger, MASIC, percolator, and iBAQ quantification parameters were as previously described (
56
). Median normalized and log10 transformed iBAQ values were used for analysis. Missing values were imputed, and differential analysis was performed using the moderated
t
test and log2 fold changes in the R package limma, with multiple-hypothesis testing corrected by the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure.
Statistical Analysis.
Statistical significance was evaluated using the two-tailed unpaired Student
t
test assuming unequal variances. For analyses involving 2 or more groups, One-Way ANOVA was used. Proteomics data were assessed using the moderated
t
test in the R package limma, with false discovery rate controlled by the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure. Data are represented as means ± SEM. Significance levels: *
P
< 0.05; **
P
< 0.01; ***
P
< 0.005; ****
P
< 0.0005; ns, not significant.
